concepts.name: Meaning of democracy, its Indian roots and the Constitution
concepts.description: What democracy is, the democratic traditions of ancient India, and the making of the Constitution of India.
concepts.idea: Democracy is government in which power lies with citizens who elect representatives; India's democratic ethos has deep historical roots.
concepts.rule: Democracy rests on freedom, equality, justice, rights and duties. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950. The Constituent Assembly (formed 1946) took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. The Constitution can be amended under Article 368.
concepts.example: Vedic assemblies (sabha, samiti, vidatha), early republican ganas and the Bauddha Samghas show early collective decision-making.

questions.q: Which one of the following correctly describes the working of the Constituent Assembly that framed the Constitution of India?
questions.a: It held eleven sessions spread over two years, eleven months and eighteen days
o: It held eleven sessions spread over two years, eleven months and eighteen days
It held eleven sessions spread over three years, two months and five days in all
It held eight sessions spread over two years, eleven months and eighteen days
It held eleven sessions spread over two years, eight months and eighteen days
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.2 Making of the Constitution, p.42: the Assembly had 11 sessions over two years, 11 months and 18 days. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.139-140, gives the same period of 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.
w: Rejected: the total period was two years, eleven months and eighteen days, not three years two months (p.42).
Rejected: the number of sessions was eleven, not eight (p.42).
Rejected: the period was eleven months and eighteen days beyond two years, not eight months (p.42).

questions.q: In the Bauddha Samghas, which the chapter cites as part of India's democratic traditions, collective decisions were reached through
questions.a: debate and discussion, with members able to choose their leader and decide matters by voting
o: debate and discussion, with members able to choose their leader and decide matters by voting
orders handed down by a hereditary head of the monastery, which the members could only accept
the verdict of the reigning king, conveyed to the community through his ministers
a vote confined to the lay donors who financed the community
questions.e: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.139: the Samgha, a monastic community established by Gautama Buddha, encouraged debate and discussion, and its members could choose their leader and decide through voting.
w: Rejected: the Samgha's leader was chosen by members, not inherited (p.139).
Rejected: the Samgha decided its own affairs; it was not directed by the king (p.139).
Rejected: it is the members of the Samgha, not lay donors, who debated and voted (p.139).

questions.q: In the Preamble to the Constitution, the word 'democratic' is used in the sense that it covers
questions.a: political democracy as well as social and economic democracy
o: political democracy as well as social and economic democracy
political democracy alone, meaning the holding of periodic elections to the legislatures
only the parliamentary form of executive, as distinct from the presidential form
direct popular rule through referendum, initiative and recall at the national level
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble, p.87: the term 'democratic' is used in the broader sense embracing not only political democracy but also social and economic democracy, a dimension Ambedkar stressed in his concluding speech of 25 November 1949. The Constitution provides for representative parliamentary democracy, not direct democracy.
w: Rejected: the book says the term goes beyond political democracy (p.87).
Rejected: the term is not limited to the type of executive; it is broader (p.87).
Rejected: India has a representative, not a direct, democracy; the devices of direct democracy are associated with Switzerland (p.87).

questions.q: Which one of the following sequences places the events in the correct chronological order?
questions.a: Objectives Resolution moved; Drafting Committee set up; Constitution adopted; Constitution comes into force
o: Objectives Resolution moved; Drafting Committee set up; Constitution adopted; Constitution comes into force
Drafting Committee set up; Objectives Resolution moved; Constitution comes into force; Constitution adopted
Constitution adopted; Objectives Resolution moved; Drafting Committee set up; Constitution comes into force
Objectives Resolution moved; Constitution adopted; Drafting Committee set up; Constitution comes into force
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.2, p.40 and p.43: Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946 and the Drafting Committee was set up on 29 August 1947. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.137, gives adoption on 26 November 1949 and commencement on 26 January 1950.
w: Rejected: the Objectives Resolution (December 1946) came before the Drafting Committee (August 1947), and adoption came before commencement.
Rejected: the Constitution was adopted only after the Objectives Resolution and the Drafting Committee.
Rejected: the Drafting Committee (August 1947) was set up long before adoption in November 1949.

questions.q: According to the chapter, the provision for amendment under Article 368 was made so that the Constitution
questions.a: remains flexible and responsive to changing needs while keeping its fundamental values
o: remains flexible and responsive to changing needs while keeping its fundamental values
stays a rigid legal code that no generation can change in any respect, whatever the needs of the time
can be rewritten by the executive by ordinance whenever Parliament is not in session
passes the power of altering it from Parliament to the judiciary on a petition by citizens
questions.e: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.140: the Assembly's debates reflect the belief that the Constitution should not be a rigid legal code but a dynamic document that can evolve through lawful amendments; Article 368 keeps it flexible and responsive. Laxmikanth Ch.12, p.199 adds that Parliament may amend any part under Article 368 without affecting the basic structure.
w: Rejected: the chapter says the opposite, a rigid code was not intended (p.140).
Rejected: amendment is a lawful process under Article 368, not an executive act (p.140).
Rejected: Article 368 does not transfer amending power to the judiciary; Parliament amends, the judiciary reviews (p.142).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. In the early republican states (ganas or samghas) the ruler acted as an independent authority and did not consult assemblies.
2. The Vedic assemblies Sabha, Samiti and Vidhata (Vidatha) involved collective decision-making.
3. A verse of the Aikyamatya Suktam in the Rigveda stresses collective thinking, shared discussion and unity of purpose.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

Statement 2 is correct: p.138-139 names them as assemblies of the Vedic period. Statement 3 is correct: p.139 cites the verse (Rigveda 10.191.3) for exactly these values. Source: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.138-139.
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.138

Consider the following statements:

1. The Constituent Assembly held its first meeting on 9 December 1946 and the Muslim League boycotted it.
2. Only 207 members were present at that first sitting.
3. After the Muslim League members withdrew, the strength of the Assembly was reduced from 389 to 299.

2. It consisted of seven members.

Consider the following statements:

1. The Objectives Resolution was unanimously adopted by the Assembly on 22 January 1947, and its modified version forms the Preamble.
2. The words 'Democratic' and 'Republic' were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
3. The Indian Independence Act of 1947 made the Constituent Assembly a fully sovereign body, which could frame any Constitution it pleased.

Which of the statements given above are correct?

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The President of India is elected directly by the people for a term of five years.
2. The term 'republic' in the Preamble indicates that India has an elected head of state for a fixed period.
3. A republic is marked by the existence of a privileged class that alone may hold the high public offices.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: p.87: the President is elected indirectly for a fixed period of five years. Statement 2 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.5 p.87. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.87: a republic means the absence of any privileged class, with all public offices open to every citizen. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble, p.87.
w: '1 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.87
'3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.87

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The State may not discriminate against a citizen solely on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, according to Article 15.
2. The second provision of Article 15, on access to shops, restaurants and wells, binds only the State and not private individuals.
3. The State is permitted to make special provisions for women and children, such as reserving seats for women in local bodies.
4. The use of the word 'only' in Article 15 means that discrimination on other grounds is not prohibited by it.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.8 p.134. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.134: it prohibits discrimination by the State and by private individuals. Statement 3 is correct: Laxmikanth p.134 lists this as the first exception. Statement 4 is correct: Laxmikanth p.134. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.8 Fundamental Rights, p.134. The Class 9 chapter, p.137, notes that the Constitution ensures no discrimination on these grounds.
w: '2, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.134
'3 and 4 only' leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.134
'1, 2, 3 and 4' includes statement 2, which is incorrect: p.134

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The Indian National Congress won 208 of the 296 seats allotted to the British Indian provinces in the 1946 elections to the Constituent Assembly.
2. The 93 seats allotted to the princely states were filled in 1946 because their rulers sent nominees at once.
3. The Muslim League won 83 seats, and the small groups and independents the remaining 15.
4. The Assembly included all important personalities of India of the time, with the exception of Mahatma Gandhi.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.2 p.40. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.40: the 93 princely-state seats were not filled because the states decided to stay away. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.40: the Muslim League won 73 seats (208 + 73 + 15 = 296). Statement 4 is correct: p.40. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.2, p.40.
w: '1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: the Muslim League won 73 seats, not 83 (p.40)
'1, 2 and 4 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect: the princely-state seats were not filled (p.40)
'2 and 3 only' includes statements 2 and 3, which are incorrect, and leaves out statements 1 and 4, which are correct: p.40

Consider the following statements:

1. The Assembly gave itself the Constitution on 26 November 1949.
2. It came into force on 26 January 1950.
3. The Constituent Assembly was formed in 1947 to draft the Constitution.

questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy p.137. Statement 2 is correct: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy p.137. questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. Ambedkar warned in his concluding speech that political democracy would not endure without social democracy underneath it.
2. In that speech, social democracy meant a way of living based on liberty, equality and fraternity together.
3. He treated liberty, equality and fraternity as three separate items of a trinity.
4. He added that liberty without equality would let the few dominate the many.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.5 p.87. Statement 2 is correct: Laxmikanth p.87. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.87: they form a union of trinity; to divorce one from the other defeats the purpose of democracy. Statement 4 is correct: Laxmikanth p.87. So 3 of 4 are correct. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble, p.87 (Ambedkar's speech of 25 November 1949).
w: 'Only one' miscounts: exactly 3 of the 4 statements are correct.
'Only two' miscounts: exactly 3 of the 4 statements are correct.
'All four' miscounts: exactly 3 of the 4 statements are correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The second reading of the Draft Constitution began on 15 November 1948 and ended on 17 October 1949.
2. The Constitution as adopted on 26 November 1949 contained a Preamble, 395 Articles and 12 Schedules.
3. Out of the 299 members of the Assembly, 284 were actually present on 26 November 1949 and signed the Constitution.
4. The general discussion on the final draft introduced on 4 November 1948 lasted ten days.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.2 p.44. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.44 gives 395 Articles and 8 Schedules at adoption. Statement 3 is correct: p.44 (284 of 299 signed). Statement 4 is incorrect: p.44 gives a general discussion of five days, till 9 November 1948. So 2 of 4 are correct. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.2, p.44.
w: 'Only one' miscounts: statements 1 and 3 are correct (2 of 4).
'Only three' miscounts: statements 2 and 4 are incorrect (the Constitution had 8 Schedules; the general discussion lasted five days).
'All four' miscounts: statements 2 and 4 are incorrect.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The democratic ethos in India did not emerge suddenly after independence.
Statement-II: Consultation in the Vedic assemblies and in the early republican states, and the later struggle against colonial rule, kept democratic ideas alive.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
questions.a: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect
Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
questions.e: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.138-139: the idea of democracy has been part of the Indian ethos since early times, and the independence struggle revived democratic ideas. Statement-II gives the historical process that makes Statement-I true.
w: Rejected: Statement-II is true and does explain Statement-I.
Rejected: Statement-II is correct.
Rejected: Statement-I is correct.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

Statement-I: The Constitution of India is a rigid legal code that cannot evolve with changing socio-political needs.
Statement-II: The Constituent Assembly's debates reflect the belief that the Constitution should be a dynamic document that can evolve through lawful amendments.

Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

o: Statement-I is incorrect but Statement-II is correct
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I

Rejected: Statement-II is correct and Statement-I is incorrect, not the reverse.

concepts.name: Principles of democracy: popular sovereignty, franchise, rule of law and rights
concepts.description: Popular sovereignty, universal adult franchise, the rule of law and the Fundamental Rights, Duties and Directive Principles.
concepts.idea: A democracy stands on certain non-negotiable principles guaranteed by the Constitution.
concepts.rule: Popular sovereignty: power lies with the people. Universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 and above may vote by secret ballot. Rule of law: no one is above the law. Six Fundamental Rights (Articles 14-32). Article 21A: right to education (2009).
concepts.example: The Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) lets citizens approach courts to enforce their rights.

questions.q: Which one of the following statements about the voting age in India is correct?
questions.a: It was lowered from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1988
o: It was lowered from 21 to 18 years by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act of 1988
It was lowered from 21 to 18 years by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1976
It was lowered from 25 to 18 years by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992
It has stood at 18 years since the Constitution was adopted and has never been changed
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.4 Salient Features, p.68: every citizen not less than 18 years of age has a right to vote; the age was reduced from 21 to 18 in 1989 by the 61st Amendment Act of 1988. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.140, states the present rule of 18 years and secret ballot.
w: Rejected: the 42nd Amendment (1976) dealt with the Preamble and other matters, not the voting age (p.68).
Rejected: the earlier age was 21, not 25, and the 73rd Amendment concerned panchayats (p.68).
Rejected: the age was 21 originally and was reduced in 1989 (p.68).

questions.q: Dicey's concept of the Rule of Law has three elements. Which of them, according to Laxmikanth, does NOT apply to the Indian system?
questions.a: The primacy of individual rights as defined by courts, since the Constitution is the source of rights in India
o: The primacy of individual rights as defined by courts, since the Constitution is the source of rights in India
The absence of arbitrary power, so that no one can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established before the ordinary courts
The equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land administered by the ordinary law courts without exemption
All three elements apply to the Indian system without any difference in the source of individual rights
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.8, p.133: Dicey's three elements are absence of arbitrary power, equality before the law, and the primacy of the rights of the individual. The first two apply to India; the third does not, because in India the Constitution is the source of individual rights.
w: Rejected: absence of arbitrary power applies to India (p.133).
Rejected: equal subjection to the ordinary law applies to India (p.133).
Rejected: the book says the third element does not apply (p.133).

questions.q: Article 21A, which provides free and compulsory education to children of six to fourteen years, was inserted into the Constitution by
o: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act of 2009 itself
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.8, p.150-151: Article 21A was added by the 86th Amendment Act of 2002; in pursuance of it Parliament later enacted the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act (2009). An ordinary Act cannot insert an Article. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.141, mentions Article 21A, the free and compulsory education of children aged 6 to 14. Note: the Class 9 chapter's 'added in 2009' refers to the RTE Act, 2009, which gave effect to Article 21A; the Article itself came in 2002.
w: Rejected: the 2009 Act was passed in pursuance of Article 21A, it did not insert the Article (p.150-151).
Rejected: the 61st Amendment lowered the voting age (p.68).
Rejected: the 42nd Amendment (1976) altered the Preamble among other things (p.85).

questions.q: Which Article did Dr B.R. Ambedkar describe as 'the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it'?
questions.a: Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies
o: Article 32, the right to constitutional remedies
Article 14, the guarantee of equality before the law
Article 21, the protection of life and personal liberty
Article 368, the power to amend the Constitution
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.8, p.158: Ambedkar called Article 32 the most important article, 'an Article without which this constitution would be a nullity'; the Supreme Court has held it to be a basic feature. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.141, names Article 32 among the remedies for violation of rights.
w: Rejected: the remark was made about Article 32 (p.158).
Rejected: the remark was made about Article 32 (p.158).
Rejected: Article 368 deals with amendment; the remark concerns the remedy of Article 32 (p.158).

questions.q: One of the following pairs of a Fundamental Right and its Articles, as listed in the chapter, is INCORRECT. Which one?
questions.a: Cultural and Educational Rights - Articles 29 to 31
o: Cultural and Educational Rights - Articles 29 to 31
Right to Equality - Articles 14 to 18, beginning with equality before law
Right to Freedom - Articles 19 to 22, beginning with the six freedoms
Right Against Exploitation - Articles 23 and 24, on trafficking and child labour
questions.e: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.141: Right to Equality (14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right Against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). The pair with Articles 29 to 31 is therefore wrong.
w: Rejected: this pair is correct (p.141).
Rejected: this pair is correct (p.141).
Rejected: this pair is correct (p.141).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. The Government of India Act, 1935 had already granted universal adult franchise before the Constitution was framed.
2. The idea of popular sovereignty means that the State derives its authority from the people.
3. Every citizen of 18 years and above has the right to vote through a secret ballot, a right known as Universal Adult Franchise.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Laxmikanth p.70 records the remark that the Constitution is essentially the 1935 Act 'with only adult franchise added'. Statement 2 is correct: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy p.140. Statement 3 is correct: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy p.140. Source: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.140; Laxmikanth Ch.4, p.68 and p.70.

1. Adult suffrage under Article 326 also governs the choice of the Rajya Sabha members from the states.
2. Under Article 325 religion, race, caste or sex cannot be a ground for keeping a person off the electoral rolls.
3. It is Article 326 that bases House of the People and state assembly polls on adult suffrage.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: Rajya Sabha members of the states are elected indirectly by the elected assembly members; Article 326 covers the Lok Sabha and the assemblies (p.89). Statement 2 is correct: Laxmikanth Ch.5 p.89. Statement 3 is correct: Laxmikanth p.89. Source: Laxmikanth Ch.5 Preamble, p.89 (political equality).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements:

1. A.V. Dicey's concept of the Rule of Law includes the absence of arbitrary power, so that no one can be punished except for a breach of law.
2. Of Dicey's three elements, the first two apply to the Indian system.
3. In the Indian system individual rights flow from court decisions, rather than from the Constitution.
4. The Court has ruled that the Rule of Law found in Article 14 cannot be destroyed even by an amendment.

concepts.name: Separation of powers, accountability and the multi-party system
concepts.description: The three organs of government, the independent judiciary, accountability and transparency, political parties and the protection of vulnerable groups.
concepts.idea: Power is divided among organs of government and checked so that no one abuses it.
concepts.rule: Legislature makes laws, executive implements them, judiciary interprets them. Accountability and transparency: RTI Act 2005, Question Hour, CAG, CIC, Lokpal, CVC. Multi-party system: the party or coalition with over 50 per cent of seats forms the government. Article 46 protects weaker sections.
concepts.example: The judiciary can review laws and amendments to ensure they agree with the Constitution.

questions.q: The doctrine of judicial review originated in the USA in Marbury versus Madison (1803). In India, according to Laxmikanth, the power of judicial review
questions.a: is conferred by the Constitution itself and has been declared a basic feature, so it cannot be curtailed even by a constitutional amendment
o: is conferred by the Constitution itself and has been declared a basic feature, so it cannot be curtailed even by a constitutional amendment
was assumed by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case and has no textual basis in the Constitution, so Parliament may regulate it by ordinary law
extends only to laws made by the Union Parliament and does not reach the legislation or executive orders of the states, which only the President may review
belongs to the Supreme Court alone, the High Courts having no power to examine the constitutionality of any law
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.27 Judicial Review, p.431: in India the Constitution itself confers the power of judicial review on the Supreme Court and the High Courts; the Supreme Court has declared it a basic feature, so it cannot be curtailed or excluded even by a constitutional amendment. It covers legislative enactments and executive orders of both the Centre and the states.
w: Rejected: the power is conferred expressly by Articles of the Constitution and is a basic feature (p.431).
Rejected: judicial review covers Central and State governments (p.431).
Rejected: both the Supreme Court and the High Courts exercise it (p.431).

He or she remains eligible for further office under the Government of India or a state after leaving the post
His or her salary and conditions of service are fixed by the Prime Minister without reference to Parliament

w: Rejected: the CAG has security of tenure and does not hold office at the President's pleasure (p.632).

Rejected: Parliament, not the Prime Minister, determines salary and service conditions (p.633).

concepts.name: Forms of democracy across the world
concepts.description: Direct and representative democracy, parliamentary and presidential systems, and examples such as India, Canada, the United Kingdom, Switzerland and the United States.
concepts.idea: Democracies share values but organise power in different ways.
concepts.rule: Representative democracy: people elect representatives. Parliamentary: the executive is part of and accountable to the legislature (India, Canada). Presidential: the executive is independent and the President is elected by the people (USA). Direct democracy: citizens directly take most decisions (Switzerland). Federalism divides power between the Union and states.
concepts.example: The United Kingdom is a parliamentary democracy with a constitutional monarchy and an unwritten constitution.

Rejected: division of power between Centre and units is federalism (p.148).

(The chapter's table, p.148, calls the Swiss President head of government; Laxmikanth's account is used here.)

Rejected: Switzerland has neither the British nor the American model (p.976).

questions.e: Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.148 and Laxmikanth Ch.95, p.953 and p.975-976, Ch.13 p.206-207: the Swiss Federal Council is plural; the UK has a constitutional monarchy and an unwritten constitution; the USA has a presidential executive; India has a parliamentary executive. concepts.name: India's living democracy and grassroots democracy
concepts.description: The scale of Indian democracy, the three-tier system, Autonomous District Councils and PESA, grassroots examples and women's voting rights and reservation.
concepts.idea: India's democracy is huge in scale and works at Union, State and local levels, giving villages a voice.
concepts.rule: India had over 96.8 crore voters in 2024, over a million polling stations, elections in 22 scheduled languages, over 2,800 registered parties. Three tiers: Union, State, Local. ADCs and PESA (1996) protect tribal areas. Article 243(d) gives one-third reservation for women in Panchayats; Article 243(t) in Municipalities.
concepts.example: Jethipura Gram Panchayat of Gujarat won the 2019 Gram Sabha award for people's participation.

concepts.name: Challenges to democracy: misinformation, inequality and the Emergency
concepts.description: Challenges such as illiteracy, fake news and inequality, the Emergency of 1975-77 and the responsibilities of citizens.
concepts.idea: Democracy needs constant care; challenges are met by informed, active citizens and constitutional safeguards.
concepts.rule: Challenges: illiteracy, misinformation and fake news, inequality, poverty, regionalism, gender inequality, discrimination, gaps in implementing laws. The Emergency of 1975-77 suspended most Fundamental Rights, censored the press and arrested leaders; elections in 1977 showed the strength of democracy.
concepts.example: Damaging public property or spreading rumours weakens democratic values.

questions.q: The National Emergency of June 1975 was proclaimed on the ground of 'internal disturbance'. Which one of the following is correct about Article 352 as it stands now?
questions.a: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance', so an Emergency can no longer rest on the latter
o: The 44th Amendment Act of 1978 substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance', so an Emergency can no longer rest on the latter
The 42nd Amendment Act of 1976 substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance', and the 44th Amendment of 1978 left that ground untouched
The 38th Amendment Act of 1975 substituted 'armed rebellion' for 'internal disturbance' just before the Emergency was proclaimed in June 1975
'Internal disturbance' remains a ground for a National Emergency, but a proclamation on it now needs approval by two-thirds of the state legislatures
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.17 Emergency Provisions, p.260: originally 'internal disturbance' was the third ground; the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 replaced it by 'armed rebellion' because it was too vague. The Class 9 Social Science chapter on Democracy, p.155, records that the 1975 Emergency was imposed on the grounds of internal disturbance.
w: Rejected: the substitution was made in 1978 by the 44th Amendment (p.260).
Rejected: the 38th Amendment (1975) dealt with different proclamations and judicial review (p.260).
Rejected: the ground was removed, and no state-legislature approval is involved (p.260).

questions.q: Since the 44th Amendment, the President can proclaim a National Emergency only after receiving
questions.a: a written recommendation from the Union Cabinet
o: a written recommendation from the Union Cabinet
the advice of the Prime Minister alone, tendered in writing
a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a special majority
a report from the Chief Justice of India on the state of the country
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.17, p.260: the President can proclaim a National Emergency only after a written recommendation from the cabinet, so that the Prime Minister alone cannot decide; in 1975 the Cabinet was informed after the proclamation as a fait accompli, and the 44th Amendment introduced the safeguard.
w: Rejected: the concurrence of the whole Cabinet is required, not merely the Prime Minister's advice (p.260).
Rejected: Parliament approves after the proclamation; it does not recommend it (p.260).
Rejected: no role is given to the Chief Justice (p.260).

questions.q: A proclamation of National Emergency must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within
questions.a: one month of its issue, by special majority
o: one month of its issue, by special majority
two months of its issue, by a simple majority in each House of Parliament
six months of its issue, by a special majority in each House of Parliament
one month of its issue, by a simple majority of the Lok Sabha
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.17, p.260-261: approval is required within one month (originally two months, reduced by the 44th Amendment) and every approving resolution must be passed by a special majority, that is a majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting; earlier a simple majority sufficed.
w: Rejected: two months and a simple majority were the pre-1978 rules (p.260-261).
Rejected: six months is the period of validity after approval, not the time for approval (p.260).
Rejected: both Houses must approve, by special majority (p.261).

questions.q: During a National Emergency, the President may suspend the right to move the courts for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, but this power cannot be exercised in respect of
questions.a: Articles 20 and 21, on conviction for offences and on life and personal liberty
o: Articles 20 and 21, on conviction for offences and on life and personal liberty
Articles 14 and 15, on equality before law and non-discrimination on stated grounds
Articles 19 and 21, on the six freedoms and on personal liberty of citizens
Articles 25 and 32, on freedom of religion and on constitutional remedies
questions.e: Laxmikanth Ch.17, p.263: the 44th Amendment provided that the President cannot suspend the right to move the court for the enforcement of the rights guaranteed by Articles 20 and 21; these remain enforceable even during an Emergency. Article 19 is suspended automatically under Article 358 (p.262-263).
w: Rejected: Articles 14 and 15 are not protected from a Presidential Order under Article 359 (p.263).
Rejected: Article 19 is not protected; it stands suspended under Article 358 in an external emergency (p.263).
Rejected: only Articles 20 and 21 are protected (p.263).
